title: Best Time to Visit Gangtok and East Sikkim
meta_description: When to visit Gangtok, Tsomgo, Nathu La and the Silk Route: clear October skies, spring rhododendrons, winter snow, monsoon landslides and festival dates.
summary: The best time to visit Gangtok is October to mid-December, when skies are clear and Kanchenjunga shows from the ridge. March to May brings rhododendrons at Tsomgo and Zuluk and warm days. December to February is cold and clear, with snow on the passes. June to September is the monsoon, with landslides on NH10.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Come between October and mid-December if you can. The monsoon has washed the haze out of the air, the mornings are cold and dry, and from Ganesh Tok, Hanuman Tok and Tashi View Point you see the Kanchenjunga range clear across the valley. The high roads to Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La and the Silk Route are usually open, and the first snow arrives on the passes in late November or December. October is also festival and holiday season, so it is busy.

March to May is the second window. Days in Gangtok are warm, around 13–22 °C, and rhododendrons flower on the road to Tsomgo and around Zuluk and Kupup from April into May. Haze builds through the day, so mountain views are a morning affair. December to February is cold and often very clear, with snow on the high roads that can close them for days. June to September is the monsoon: green, wet, cheap and hard to move around in.

Gangtok itself, at about 1,650 m, is never extreme. What changes with the seasons is everything above it: Tsomgo at 3,753 m, Nathu La at 4,310 m and the Silk Route at 2,900–4,000 m are cold for most of the year and snowbound for part of it. Choose your month by what you want to do up there.

sections.heading: Gangtok month by month
paras: Temperatures are rough ranges for Gangtok town. Tsomgo, Nathu La, Kupup and Gnathang are 10–20 °C colder, and below freezing at night for much of the year.

sections.heading: October to mid-December: the clear season
paras: This is when Gangtok looks the way the posters promise. On most mornings the Kanchenjunga range stands on the western skyline from first light until cloud builds around 10 or 11 am. Tsomgo Lake is blue and unfrozen in October and early November, and Nathu La is cold but usually open from Wednesday to Sunday. The Silk Route is at its best, with the zigzag road below Thambi View Point sharp in clear air and a good chance of seeing Kanchenjunga at dawn from Lungthung.

The catch is crowds. Durga Puja, Dashain, Diwali and Tihar bring holidaymakers from Kolkata and the plains, and Gangtok's rooms, shared jeeps and permit-tour seats fill up. Book a month or more ahead for the Puja weeks. November, once the festivals pass, is our favourite: steady weather, lower rates and the first dusting of snow on the passes. Early December is similar, colder and quieter, until the Christmas and New Year rush.
Losoong, the Sikkimese harvest new year, falls in December, and the Tsuklakhang royal chapel holds its Kagyed cham dances in the same month. Ask locally for the year's dates.

sections.heading: March to May: rhododendrons and warm days
paras: Spring brings Sikkim's state tree into flower. Rhododendrons bloom in red, pink and white on the road to Tsomgo, around Kupup and Gnathang, and on the slopes above Zuluk, usually from April into May, a little later the higher you go. Lower down, magnolias flower in March and the orchids at the Gangtok flower shows peak in spring. Gangtok is pleasant for walking, and evenings on MG Marg are mild.

Mountain views are less reliable. Haze rises from the plains by mid-morning, so plan viewpoints for dawn. Snow lingers on the high roads into April and sometimes May, and Tsomgo can stay partly frozen into spring. May brings the school holidays and Gangtok's busiest weeks after October; book ahead. Saga Dawa, the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist year, often falls in late May or June, with processions in Gangtok.

sections.heading: December to February: snow and clear cold
paras: Winter is cold, clear and cheap outside the Christmas and New Year week. Gangtok drops to around 4–6 °C at night, and old hotels are chilly, so ask for a heater. The reward is some of the clearest skies of the year and snow at Tsomgo, Baba Mandir, Nathu La, Kupup and Gnathang. Tsomgo usually freezes over. For many Indian families, seeing snow is the point of the trip, and this is when you can.

Snow also closes roads. After a heavy fall the army and the Border Roads Organisation clear the routes, but Nathu La and the Silk Route can stay shut for days, and permits are not issued until they reopen. Keep at least one spare day in Gangtok. Hire snow boots and a coat at the Tsomgo road stalls for ₹100–200 if you need them. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or March, with dances and prayers at Rumtek.

sections.heading: June to September: the monsoon
paras: The monsoon reaches Sikkim in June and stays until September. Rain falls most days, often heavily, clouds hide the mountains and landslides block roads for hours or days. NH10, the main road up the Teesta from Siliguri, has had repeated closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood, and monsoon closures are now common; traffic then detours via Kalimpong. North Sikkim roads have had long closures too. Check current status before you travel.

There are reasons to come. Rooms are at their cheapest, Gangtok is green and quiet, and the town has enough monasteries, cafés and museums to fill wet days. Pang Lhabsol, the festival honouring Kanchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity, falls in August or September, with masked dances at Tsuklakhang. If you come, keep your plans flexible, add buffer days before trains and flights, and treat Tsomgo or the Silk Route as a bonus if the weather allows.
list: Carry a proper raincoat and quick-dry clothes.
Start any drive early; afternoon rain brings more slides.
Book refundable rooms and tickets where you can.

sections.heading: Choosing by what you want
paras: If you want Kanchenjunga, come in November. If you want snow, come in January or February and keep a spare day. If you want rhododendrons on the Silk Route, come in late April or early May. If you want festivals, plan around Losar in February or March, Saga Dawa in May or June, Pang Lhabsol in late summer, or Losoong in December. If you want the lowest prices with roads mostly open, come in late February, early March or the first half of December.

Two more things shape any season. The first is the plains' holiday calendar: Durga Puja and Diwali in October or November, Christmas to New Year, and the May–June school holidays decide when Gangtok is full far more than the weather does, so check those dates before you fix yours. The second is the road. NH10 has had repeated closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood, and the North Sikkim roads beyond Gangtok have been shut for long periods, so even in the dry months keep one spare day and check current status before you travel. Whatever the month, pack layers: a sunny October afternoon on MG Marg and a frozen morning at Tsomgo can fall on the same day.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit Gangtok?
faqs.a: November is the steadiest month: clear skies, Kanchenjunga visible most mornings, open roads to Tsomgo and Nathu La and fewer crowds than October. October is equally clear but busy with Puja holidaymakers. April is the best spring month, with rhododendrons on the high roads but more haze over the mountains.

faqs.q: When can I see snow in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Gangtok town rarely gets snow. You see it at Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir, Nathu La and the Silk Route, usually from December to March and sometimes into April or May. January and February are the surest months. Heavy snow can close these roads for days, so keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to visit Gangtok in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Gangtok town is safe, but travel in and out is unpredictable. Landslides block NH10 and the high roads, sometimes for days, and NH10 has had repeated closures since the October 2023 flood. If you come between June and September, keep plans flexible, add buffer days and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Nathu La open in winter?
faqs.a: Nathu La can be visited in winter when the road is clear, but heavy snow often closes it for days, and permits are not issued while it is shut. It is commonly reported closed to tourists on Mondays and Tuesdays all year. Book through a registered operator and check current status before you travel.

Tsomgo usually freezes in the winter months, from about January into March, and it can stay partly frozen into April or May after a hard winter. It is unfrozen and blue from about June to December, with the clearest skies in October and November. The road can close after snow.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom in East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Usually from April into May on the road to Tsomgo and on the Silk Route around Zuluk, Kupup and Gnathang, a little later at higher altitudes. Lower forests flower from March. The exact timing shifts with the winter, so ask a Gangtok driver or homestay before you plan around the flowers.

faqs.q: Is Gangtok very cold in December?
faqs.a: Gangtok is cold but manageable in December, around 6–15 °C by day and colder at night, and many hotels lack central heating, so ask for a heater. Tsomgo, Nathu La and the Silk Route are well below freezing. Pack thermals, a down jacket, a warm hat and gloves.

faqs.q: When are the festivals in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or March; Saga Dawa in May or June; Pang Lhabsol, honouring Kanchenjunga, in August or September; and Losoong, the Sikkimese new year, with Kagyed cham at Tsuklakhang, in December. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

June to August is cheapest, but it is the monsoon, with landslides and rare views. For low prices with fair weather, come in late February, early March or the first half of December, avoiding the Puja, Diwali, Christmas and May school holiday weeks, when rates rise by a third or more.
